title: Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law
content:
# Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law

## Imperial China (pre-1911)
- Whether civil law existed in Imperial China is **debatable**: scholars such as **Liang Chichao (梁啟超)** and **Wang Boqi (王伯琦)** argued civil law (as distinct from criminal law) did not exist, while **Yang Honglie (楊鴻烈)** held the opposite view.
- Beyond dispute: **no civil code ever existed** in Imperial China, though there was **separate legislation on marriage and debt**.

## Late Qing: first draft civil code
- **1902**: Emperor Guang Xu formed a team to draft a civil code modelled on **Continental European codes**.
- Drafting ran **1908–1910**, producing the **Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (《大清民律草案》)** — the first civil code in China's history, though only in draft form.
- **Never enacted**: the Qing Dynasty was overthrown shortly afterwards.

## Republican era: first enacted civil code
- **April 1927**: National Government established; **December 1928**: the legislature (Legislative Yuan) took charge of drafting.
- **January 1929**: Drafting Committee of the Civil Code set up; compilation began **February 1929**.
- **26 December 1930**: the **Civil Law of the Republic of China (《中華民國民法》)** promulgated — the first enacted civil code in Chinese history, containing **detailed contract law provisions**.

## Post-1949 People's Republic
- **1954**: drafting of a new civil code began; a draft was completed **December 1956**, but enactment was blocked by the **antirightist movements and the Cultural Revolution**; political unrest ended in **1978**.
- Rather than revisiting the old draft, China legislated on contract law **piecemeal** to serve the economic reform starting 1979:
  - **Economic Contract Law (1981)**
  - **Foreign Economic Contract Law (1985)**
  - **Technology Contract Law (1987)**
- The **General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL, 1985)** is **not a civil code** — only "general principles", like the introductory chapter of a still-unfinished code.
- The three contract statutes were **not comprehensive**: they contained **contradictory provisions** and **overlapping scopes**.

## The 1999 unified Contract Law
- **1993**: drafting of a unified Contract Law began to replace the three statutes; drafters were largely **legal academics**.
- Extensive reference to international and comparative sources: **UNIDROIT Principles (PICC)**, **CISG**, **Principles of European Contract Law (PECL)**, the **French and German civil codes**, and **English common law**.
- **Passed 15 March 1999, effective 1 October 1999**; supplemented by the **Supreme People's Court Interpretation on Several Issues Regarding the Application of the Contract Law** and other judicial interpretations (e.g. on technology and construction contracts).
- The 1999 Contract Law has **not been revised** since promulgation (as of the source text).

## Timeline at a glance
```mermaid
timeline
    title Chinese Contract Law: key milestones
    1902 : Emperor Guang Xu orders a civil code drafted on the Continental European model
    1908-1910 : Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (《大清民律草案》) — first draft civil code, never enacted
    1930 : Civil Law of the Republic of China (《中華民國民法》) — first enacted civil code, with detailed contract provisions
    1954-1956 : PRC civil code drafting; draft completed but not enacted (antirightist movements, Cultural Revolution)
    1981/1985/1987 : Economic Contract Law, Foreign Economic Contract Law, Technology Contract Law (piecemeal, overlapping)
    1985 : General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL) — general principles only, not a code
    1993 : Drafting of unified Contract Law begins, drawing on PICC, CISG, PECL, French/German codes, English common law
    1999 : Contract Law of the PRC passed 15 March, effective 1 October; supplemented by SPC judicial interpretations
```
